extracted.intended_audience: Federal agency NEPA practitioners, environmental review staff, and agency decisionmakers responsible for preparing or supervising NEPA analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and best-practice criteria for Federal agencies to plan, conduct, document, and publicize NEPA reviews (categorical exclusions, environmental assessments, and environmental impact statements), including roles, timing, public engagement, and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient process
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall improve efficiency of their NEPA processes by using a range of measures to avoid unnecessary delay and duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures include: establishing categorical exclusions for actions that normally do not have significant effects; using a finding of no significant impact when appropriate; integrating NEPA into early planning; engaging in interagency cooperation before or during preparation of documents; ensuring swift and fair resolution of lead agency disputes; using scoping to identify important issues early; meeting appropriate deadlines; preparing environmental documents early; integrating NEPA with other environmental review and consultation requirements; eliminating duplication with State, Tribal, and local procedures and other Federal procedures (joint preparation or adoption of documents); combining environmental documents with other documents; and, where applicable, using accelerated procedures for proposals for legislation. (See §1500.5(a)-(l).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authority and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency shall interpret NEPA as a supplement to its existing authority and review policies, procedures, and regulations to ensure compliance with NEPA to the fullest extent possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must view policies and missions in light of NEPA's national environmental objectives and revise procedures as necessary. The phrase 'to the fullest extent possible' means agencies must comply with NEPA unless an activity is exempted by law or compliance is impossible. (See §1500.6.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of planning part (1501.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate the NEPA process into agency planning early, provide for early engagement, ensure swift resolution of interagency disputes, focus study on important issues, and promote accountability via deadlines and schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes include facilitating appropriate consideration of NEPA policies, promoting efficiency, reducing delay, early engagement with other governments and interested persons, identifying important environmental issues early and deemphasizing unimportant issues, narrowing scope of review, and establishing schedules. (See §1501.1.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply NEPA early in the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should integrate NEPA with other planning and authorization at the earliest reasonable time so environmental effects are considered in planning and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each agency shall: (1) use a systematic, interdisciplinary approach integrating natural and social sciences and environmental design arts; (2) identify environmental effects and values in adequate detail so decisionmakers can weigh them alongside economic and technical analyses; (3) study, develop, and describe appropriate alternatives where conflicts exist; and (4) provide for applicant-planned actions by advising applicants about foreseeable studies, consulting early with State, Tribal, local governments and interested persons, and commencing NEPA at the earliest reasonable time. Whenever practicable, agencies should review and publish environmental documents at the same time as other planning documents. (See §1501.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine applicability of NEPA (threshold test)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a threshold matter, an agency shall assess whether NEPA applies to the proposed activity or decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing applicability, agencies should determine whether: (1) the action is exempted from NEPA by law; (2) compliance would clearly and fundamentally conflict with another Federal law; (3) the action is not a major Federal action (§1508.1(w)); (4) the action is not a final agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act; or (5) the action is non-discretionary such that the agency lacks authority to consider environmental factors. (See §1501.3(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of action and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When NEPA applies, agencies shall consider the scope of the proposed action and its effects to inform the appropriate level of review and whether aspects are non-discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public engagement and scoping mechanisms to inform scope. Evaluate related proposals or parts of proposals in a single review where closely related. Do not avoid a significance determination by wrongly terming an action temporary or by improperly segmenting an action. Consider connected actions (those that automatically trigger other actions, cannot proceed without other actions, or are interdependent) in the same NEPA review. Agencies may use any reliable data source and are not required to undertake new research unless essential to a reasoned choice and reasonable in cost/time. (See §1501.3(b)-(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of NEPA review (CX / EA / EIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall determine whether a proposed action is appropriately categorically excluded, appropriate for an environmental assessment, or requires an environmental impact statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should determine if the action: (1) is appropriately categorically excluded (§1501.4); (2) is not likely to have significant effects or significance is unknown and is appropriate for an EA (§1501.5); or (3) is likely to have significant effects and requires an EIS (part 1502). (See §1501.3(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance determination — context and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether an adverse effect is significant, agencies must examine both the context of the action and the intensity of the effect and consider duration and timing of effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may not offset an action's adverse effects with other beneficial effects to determine significance. Analyze context across geographic scales (global to local) and duration (short- and long-term). Analyze intensity using factors as applicable and in relationship to one another, including: (i) degree of adverse effects on public health and safety; (ii) adverse effects on unique characteristics (historic/cultural resources, parks, Tribal sacred sites, wetlands, etc.); (iii) potential to violate laws or be inconsistent with protective policies; (iv) degree of uncertainty in potential effects; (v) effects on National Register-eligible resources; (vi) effects on endangered/threatened species or critical habitat; (vii) effects on communities with environmental justice concerns; and (viii) adverse effects on Tribal rights reserved by treaties, statutes, or Executive Orders. (See §1501.3(d)(1)-(2) and examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical exclusions (establishment and application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall establish categorical exclusions for categories of actions that normally do not have significant effects and may apply them unless extraordinary circumstances exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may establish CXs individually or jointly. If a proposed action falls under a CX, the agency must evaluate for extraordinary circumstances; where such circumstances exist the agency may still apply the CX only after analysis showing no potential for significant effects or by modifying the action to avoid such effects, and must document and publicly provide that determination. Agencies may establish CXs through land use plans, programmatic documents, or equivalent decisions if they: provide the Council an opportunity to review before public comment; provide notice and opportunity for public comment; substantiate that the category normally does not have significant effects; identify extraordinary circumstances; establish a process to determine applicability to specific actions; and publish the list of CXs on the agency website. CXs may be geographic-limited, time-limited, include mitigation measures with monitoring/enforcement, or provide criteria for expiration (e.g., thresholds exceeded, proximity/time clustering, or changed environmental conditions). Agencies may adopt another agency's CX with consultation, public notification, an evaluation for extraordinary circumstances, and publication of documentation. (See §1501.4(a)-(e).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental assessment (EA) requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An EA must be prepared for actions not likely to have significant effects or when significance is unknown unless a CX applies or an EIS is prepared; EAs may also be prepared to assist planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An EA shall: (1) briefly provide sufficient evidence and analysis to determine whether to prepare an EIS or a FONSI; (2) briefly discuss purpose and need, alternatives as required by NEPA section 102(2)(H), and environmental effects of the proposed action and alternatives; (3) list Federal, State, Tribal, and local governments and persons consulted; and (4) provide a unique identification number for tracking. Agencies shall commence EAs as soon as practicable after receiving an application, invite public comment on drafts and consider comments in the final EA, involve public and governments to the extent practicable, and generally limit the EA text to 75 pages (excluding citations and appendices). Agencies should supplement incomplete/ongoing major Federal actions when there are substantial changes or new information, may prepare supplements to further NEPA purposes, may reevaluate an EA to determine whether a supplemental EA or new FONSI/EIS is needed, and generally should apply §1502.21 and may apply other Part 1502 and 1503 provisions as appropriate. (See §1501.5(a)-(k).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) and mitigated FONSI
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing an EA, the agency shall prepare a FONSI if no significant effects are found, a mitigated FONSI if mitigation will avoid significance, or an EIS if significant effects are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency shall make the FONSI available to the affected public as specified in §1501.9(c)(5). In two circumstances (action normally requiring an EIS or an action without precedent), the agency shall make the FONSI available for public review for 30 days before determining whether to prepare an EIS and before the action may begin. The FONSI shall include or incorporate the EA and need not repeat the EA discussion if incorporated. The FONSI must state the authority for any mitigation and applicable monitoring/enforcement provisions; a mitigated FONSI must state enforceable mitigation commitments and the authority to enforce them (e.g., permit terms, incidental take statement), and the agency shall prepare a monitoring and compliance plan for mitigation consistent with §1505.3(c). (See §1501.6(a)-(d).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead agency designation and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: When more than one Federal agency proposes or is involved in the same action or closely related group of actions, a lead agency shall supervise preparation of the EA or EIS; agencies must promptly determine which will be lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may have joint lead agencies. Participating Federal agencies shall determine lead agency by letter or memorandum, considering factors listed in descending importance: (1) magnitude of agency's involvement; (2) project approval/disapproval authority; (3) expertise concerning environmental effects; (4) duration of involvement; and (5) sequence of involvement. Agencies should resolve lead designation without delay; any affected party may request designation and the Council will decide if agencies can't agree (with specified submission and timing procedures). The lead agency should evaluate proposals requiring more than one Federal agency in a single EIS or EA and, where practicable, issue joint RODs or joint FONSIs. The lead agency's duties regarding cooperating agencies include requesting participation early, considering cooperating agencies' analyses, meeting with them on request, and determining purpose/need and alternatives in consultation with cooperating agencies. (See §1501.7.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperating agency roles and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperating agencies (Federal agencies with jurisdiction by law or special expertise; State, Tribal, or local agencies by agreement) participate early and provide expertise to the NEPA process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each cooperating agency shall: participate at the earliest practicable time; participate in scoping (§1502.4); on lead agency request, assume responsibility for developing information and preparing environmental analyses (including parts of EIS/EA where it has special expertise); provide staff support to enhance interdisciplinary capability; normally use its own funds (lead should fund major activities it requests to the extent funds permit); consult in developing/updating the schedule and meet it, elevating schedule-impacting issues as necessary; meet the lead agency's schedule for providing comments; and to the maximum extent practicable, jointly issue environmental documents with the lead agency. A cooperating agency may decline requested involvement due to other commitments but must submit a copy of the reply to the Council and the lead agency's senior official. Federal agencies may appeal denial of cooperating agency designation to the Council. Indigenous Knowledge is explicitly included as relevant special expertise. (See §1501.8.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and governmental engagement — purpose and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Public engagement is intended to inform the public of proposed actions, allow meaningful engagement in the NEPA process, and ensure decisionmakers are informed by public views; governmental engagement identifies affected governments and invites them as cooperating agencies and to participate as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must determine appropriate methods of engagement for each proposed action and use engagement to inform level of review and scope consistent with §1501.3; EISs must also comply with scoping requirements (§1502.4). (See §1501.9(a)-(b).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Outreach and notification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall invite likely affected agencies and governments to participate early, engage likely affected or interested members of the public (including those likely to disagree), and select outreach methods appropriate to affected entities, scale, public interest, and access needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must: invite Federal, State, Tribal, and local governments to participate (including as cooperating agencies); conduct early engagement with interested public (unless narrow exception applies); consider outreach methods based on access to electronic media and primary languages; publish notification of proposed actions to be analyzed in an EIS (notice of intent); provide public notification of NEPA hearings/meetings and document availability; notify those who requested notification for a particular action or regular notifications; publish Federal Register notice for actions of national concern; for local-concern actions, use distribution through State/Tribal procedures, local newspapers, other local media, community organizations, newsletters, direct mailings to owners/occupants, on/off-site postings, and electronic media (agency website, dashboard, email lists, social media). Agencies should establish email notification lists or similar. EISs, comments, and underlying documents should be made available under FOIA and without charge to the extent practicable. (See §1501.9(c)(1)-(6) and subparts (i)-(iii) and (A)-(I).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public meetings and hearings format and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall hold public hearings/meetings whenever appropriate or required, and may conduct them electronically except where another format is required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting format (in-person, virtual, formal hearing, listening session), agencies must consider needs of affected communities. For electronic/virtual hearings, agencies must allow electronic, mail, or other appropriate methods for submitting comments. Agencies should make a draft environmental document available at least 15 days in advance when it is the subject of a hearing or meeting unless the meeting's purpose is information gathering for document development. (See §1501.9(d).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency procedures to engage public
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies shall make diligent efforts to engage the public in preparing and implementing their NEPA procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are expected to include public engagement in their internal NEPA procedures (§1507.3) and to exert diligent efforts to involve publics in both preparation and implementation. (See §1501.9(e).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and scheduling for NEPA reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead agencies shall set action-appropriate deadlines and schedules and complete EAs and EISs within specified timeframes unless extended in writing for necessary reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies shall set deadlines and schedules appropriate to individual actions in consultation with joint lead, cooperating, and participating agencies and applicants. Agencies shall complete: (1) EAs within 1 year unless the lead agency extends the deadline in writing (with new deadline only as much additional time as necessary); and (2) EISs within 2 years unless extended in writing (with same extension constraints). These deadlines are measured from the sooner of: when the agency determines that NEPA requires an EA/EIS; when the agency notifies an applicant that an application is complete (e.g., right-of-way); or when the agency issues a notice of intent. The deadlines are measured to specific endpoints: for EAs, the date the EA is published or made available pre-decisional or the date a notice of intent to prepare an EIS is issued; for EISs, the EPA publication of availability of the final EIS or the date the final EIS is made available pre-decisional, consistent with §1506.10(c)(1). (See §1501.10(a)-(b).)
